claim: Mice solve the olfactory search task using concentration gradient cues and do not require stereo olfaction for performance.
source: Mice solve this task using concentration gradient cues and do not require stereo olfaction for performance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing performance varies with concentration gradient (Figure 2D), performance is equal across different absolute concentrations at fixed gradient (Figure 2E), and naris occlusion does not significantly impact performance (Figure 2F).

claim: During task performance, respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision.
source: During task performance, respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing kinematic rhythms lock to sniffing with tens of milliseconds precision (Figure 5).

claim: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals.
source: This synchrony is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals, suggesting that sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than simply a constant accompaniment to fast breathing.
evidence: Supported by data showing kinematic synchrony is significantly reduced during ITI compared to within-trial periods (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Movement motifs fall into two clusters, which correspond to investigation and approach states.
source: Motifs fall into two clusters, which correspond to investigation and approach states.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of the Markov transition matrix that separated motifs into two groups with distinct properties (Figure 7A).

claim: Investigation motifs lock precisely to sniffing, such that individual motifs preferentially occur at specific phases of the sniff cycle.
source: Investigation motifs lock precisely to sniffing, such that the individual motifs preferentially occur at specific phases of the sniff cycle.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing investigation motif onsets are significantly modulated in both time and phase coordinates relative to sniffing (Figure 8).

claim: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff strategy for gradient sensing.
source: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff strategy for gradient sensing.
evidence: Supported by occupancy mapping showing correct trials feature increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline (Figure 10G), where gradients are steepest.

claim: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session of the 100:0 condition.
source: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session (Figure 2B; binomial test, p<0.05 for 24 out of 25 mice, 75 ± 9.2% correct, mean ± sd).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral performance data from first training session.

claim: Within four sessions, most animals exceeded 80% performance in the 100:0 condition.
source: Within four sessions, most animals exceeded 80% performance (19 out of 26).
evidence: Supported by behavioral performance data across training sessions.

claim: Mice trained to search pinene plumes generalize their search behavior to vanillin, a novel odorant.
source: We found no differences in performance between vanillin and pinene sessions for these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.827, n = 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing performance with pinene versus vanillin.

claim: Trigeminal chemosensation is not necessary for performance in the olfactory search task.
source: We chose vanillin as the novel odorant because, unlike pinene, vanillin does not activate the trigeminal fibers of the nose (Cometto-Muñiz and Abraham, 2010; Doty et al., 1978; Hummel et al., 2009). Thus, we could test whether trigeminal chemosensation is necessary for performance in our task. We found no differences in performance between vanillin and pinene sessions for these mice
evidence: Inferred from equal performance with vanillin (which does not activate trigeminal system) and pinene (which does), supported by citations about vanillin's lack of trigeminal activation.

claim: On odor omission probe trials (0:0), mice performed at chance level.
source: On these probe trials, mice performed at chance (binomial test, p=0.9989)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of performance on 0:0 trials.

claim: Odor omission trials resulted in longer trial durations and more tortuous trajectories than non-probe trials.
source: with longer trial durations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and more tortuous trajectories (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) than on non-probe trials (Figure 2C; n = 19, all data from 80:20 condition with probe trials).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of trial duration and path tortuosity between probe and non-probe trials, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Performance drops with decreasing concentration ratio (ΔC).
source: Performance drops with the concentration ratio (ΔC), consistent with our reasoning that mice would use odor gradient cues in this task (Figure 2D; pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p<0.05, n = 15).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of performance across different concentration ratios, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Varying the concentration ratio from 80:20 to 60:40 did not affect trial duration or path tortuosity.
source: Varying the concentration ratio from 80:20 to 60:40 did not affect trial duration or path tortuosity, defined as actual path length divided by direct path length (Figure 2D; pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing trial duration and tortuosity between 80:20 and 60:40 conditions.

claim: Trial duration and path tortuosity were slightly but statistically significantly longer in the 100:0 condition compared to other conditions.
source: However, trial duration and path tortuosity were slightly, but statistically significantly, longer in the 100:0 condition (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of trial metrics across concentration conditions.

claim: Mice performed equally well in both 90:30 and 30:10 conditions in the first session.
source: In both conditions, mice performed equally well in the first session (Figure 2E; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.465, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of performance between 90:30 and 30:10 conditions in first session.

claim: Equal performance in 90:30 and 30:10 conditions indicates that odor gradients guide olfactory search under these conditions.
source: These results indicate that odor gradients guide olfactory search under these conditions.
evidence: Inferred from equal performance in conditions where absolute concentration judgment would give opposite answers, supported by experimental data.

claim: Naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity.
source: We found that naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of performance and tortuosity across naris occlusion, sham, and no procedure conditions.

claim: Naris occlusion resulted in a slight but statistically significant increase in trial duration compared to the no-stitch condition.
source: When compared with the no-stitch condition, the naris stitch condition resulted in a slight, but statistically significant, increase in trial duration (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of trial duration between naris stitch and no-stitch conditions.

claim: The increase in trial duration with naris occlusion may be a result of undergoing a surgical procedure rather than the occlusion itself.
source: This is not true when the stitch condition is compared with the sham condition (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05), indicating this may be a result of undergoing a surgical procedure.
evidence: Inferred from lack of significant difference between stitch and sham conditions, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Stereo comparison is not necessary for performance in this olfactory search task.
source: These overall results indicate that stereo comparison is not necessary in this task (Figure 2F; n = 13)
evidence: Supported by naris occlusion experimental data showing no significant performance deficit.

claim: Temporal comparisons across sniffs play a larger role than stereo comparisons under the task conditions.
source: and that temporal comparisons across sniffs (Catania, 2013; Parabucki et al., 2019) play a larger role under our task conditions.
evidence: Inferred from naris occlusion results and supported by citations to previous work on temporal comparisons.

claim: The overall sniff pattern is consistent across trials, with an inhalation just before trial initiation followed by a long exhalation or pause at the beginning of the trial.
source: The overall sniff pattern was consistent across trials, with an inhalation just before trial initiation followed by a long exhalation or pause at the beginning of the trial (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sniff patterns across trials, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mice perform a rapid burst of sniffs after trial initiation, then sniff more slowly as they approach the target.
source: Next, the mice performed a rapid burst of sniffs, then sniffed more slowly as they approached the target (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sniff rate over the course of trials, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhalation and sniff durations are shorter during trials than during inter-trial intervals.
source: In this active behavioral state, inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during ITIs (p<<0.01 for all mice; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3B, C)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of sniff parameters between trials and ITIs, shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Sniff durations during the task are strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents.
source: and strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison to previous literature on sniff durations in head-fixed rodents, supported by citations.

claim: After the decision, there is a second rapid burst of sniffing followed by a long exhalation or pause during reward anticipation and retrieval.
source: After the decision, there is a second rapid burst of sniffing followed by a long exhalation or pause during reward anticipation and retrieval (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sniff patterns after decision point, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mice move their nose through tortuous trajectories that are not stereotyped from trial to trial.
source: During this sniffing behavior, the mice moved their nose through tortuous trajectories that were not stereotyped from trial to trial (Figure 3D, E; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by video tracking data showing variable trajectories across trials, shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: Individual mice show position biases, but these biases are not systematic across mice.
source: Although individual mice showed position biases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), these biases were not systematic across mice
evidence: Supported by analysis of individual mouse occupancy patterns shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The across-mouse mean occupancy distribution is evenly distributed across the two sides of the arena.
source: so that the across-mouse mean occupancy distribution was evenly distributed across the two sides of the arena (Figure 3F; n = 19).
evidence: Supported by analysis of mean occupancy across mice, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Sniff rate is highest near the initiation port and slower on the approach to target.
source: Consistent with this sniffing and movement pattern, the sniff rate was highest near the initiation port and slower on the approach to target (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by spatial analysis of sniff rate shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Measures of active sampling are not statistically distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions.
source: These measures of active sampling were not statistically distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons of sniffing and movement measures across experimental conditions.

claim: Active sampling measures change significantly on odor omission probe trials, with more fast sniffing and head turns overall.
source: but changed significantly on odor omission probe trials, with more fast sniffing and head turns overall.
evidence: Supported by comparison of sampling behavior between probe and non-probe trials.

claim: Nose speed accelerates during exhalation, peaks at inhalation onset, and decelerates during inhalation.
source: On average, nose speed accelerates during exhalation, peaks at inhalation onset, and decelerates during inhalation (Figure 5Ai).
evidence: Supported by analysis of nose speed aligned to sniff cycle, shown in Figure 5Ai.

claim: Head yaw velocity reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation, decelerates and moves centripetally over the course of inhalation.
source: Head yaw velocity, which we define as toward or away (Figure 4; centripetal or centrifugal) from the body-head axis, reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation, decelerates and moves centripetally over the course of inhalation (Figure 5Aii).
evidence: Supported by analysis of yaw velocity aligned to sniff cycle, shown in Figure 5Aii.

claim: Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation.
source: The Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation (Figure 5Aiii).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Z-velocity aligned to sniff cycle, shown in Figure 5Aiii.

claim: Kinematic modulations are absent from trial-shuffled data.
source: These modulations were absent from trial-shuffled data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; permutation test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by permutation testing comparing real data to shuffled controls, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Precise cycle-by-cycle synchronization between kinematic rhythms and sniffing can be a feature of goal-directed odor-guided behavior.
source: Our findings show that precise cycle-by-cycle synchronization can also be a feature of goal-directed odor-guided behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing sniff-synchronized movement during olfactory search task.

claim: Sniff synchrony is significantly reduced during the inter-trial interval compared to within trials.
source: For nose speed, yaw velocity, and Z-velocity, sniff synchrony is significantly reduced during the ITI when the mouse is returning from the reward port to initiate the next trial, even when the mouse is sniffing rapidly.
evidence: Supported by comparison of kinematic modulation between trial and ITI periods.

claim: Modulations in nose speed during ITI are slightly different than trial-shuffled data, showing that sniff-synchronized movement is not totally absent during the ITI.
source: Modulations in nose speed were slightly different than trial-shuffled data, showing that sniff-synchronized movement is not totally absent during the ITI
evidence: Supported by comparison of nose speed modulation during ITI to shuffled controls.

claim: Modulations in yaw velocity and Z-velocity during ITI are indistinguishable from trial-shuffled data.
source: whereas modulations in yaw velocity and Z-velocity were indistinguishable from trial-shuffled data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of yaw and Z-velocity modulation during ITI to shuffled controls.

claim: The difference in sniff synchrony between within-trial and between-trial periods is not contingent on the mouse's slower nose speed during the ITI.
source: This difference between within-trial and between-trial sniff synchrony was not contingent on the mouse's slower nose speed during the ITI (Figure 5A). Kinematic synchrony was the same when only periods of high-speed nose movement in the ITI are included in the analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis controlling for nose speed differences between trial and ITI periods.

claim: Sniff-synchronized movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than an inevitable biomechanical accompaniment to fast sniffing.
source: This reduction of kinematic synchrony when the mouse is not performing the task suggests that sniff-synchronized movement is not an inevitable biomechanical accompaniment to fast sniffing, but rather reflects a strategic behavioral state.
evidence: Inferred from differential sniff synchrony during task versus ITI periods, supported by experimental data.

claim: Mice execute sniff-synchronized movement after premature attempts at trial initiation, despite the absence of experimenter-applied odor stimulus.
source: Further support for this idea comes from analyzing time intervals when the mouse attempts to initiate a trial before the end of the ITI. After such premature attempts at trial initiation, the mice execute sniff-synchronized movement, despite the absence of the experimenter-applied odor stimulus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of movement during premature trial initiation attempts.

claim: Sniff synchrony changes dramatically in the time interval between crossing the virtual decision line and entering the reward port.
source: Lastly, sniff synchrony changes dramatically in the time interval between crossing the virtual decision line and entering the reward port, when odor is still present yet the animal has committed to a decision (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sniff synchrony after decision commitment.

claim: Sniff synchronous movement is a proactive, odor-seeking strategy rather than a reactive, odor-gated reflex.
source: Taken together, our observations indicate that sniff synchronous movement is a proactive, odor-seeking strategy rather than a reactive, odor-gated reflex.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing context-dependent deployment of sniff-synchronized movement.

claim: AR-HMM models define discrete movement patterns, or 'motifs', that recur throughout the dataset.
source: These models defined discrete movement patterns, or 'motifs', that recur throughout our dataset (e.g., Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by AR-HMM modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The cross-validated log-likelihood of AR-HMM fits continued to rise up to 100 motifs.
source: We fit different AR-HMMs each constrained to find a particular number of motifs (between 6 and 100) and found that the cross-validated log-likelihood of these fits continued to rise up to 100 motifs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by model comparison analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motifs extracted by the AR-HMM have interpretable spatiotemporal trajectories on average.
source: The motifs extracted by this model have interpretable spatiotemporal trajectories on average (Figure 6B, Video 5)
evidence: Supported by visualization of average motif trajectories in Figure 6B.

claim: Averaging motif trajectories masks considerable across-instance variability.
source: although averaging masks considerable across-instance variability (Video 6).
evidence: Supported by video evidence showing variability in motif instances.

claim: Across trials for a given mouse, motifs occur in consistent but non-stereotyped sequences.
source: Across trials for a given mouse, motifs occurred in consistent but non-stereotyped sequences (Figure 6C, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis of motif sequences shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The AR-HMM identifies consistent behavioral features as motifs across mice.
source: Across mice, the model identified consistent behavioral features as motifs (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by cross-mouse comparison of motifs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Most mice are uniquely identifiable from how they sequence motifs across trials.
source: but most mice were uniquely identifiable from how they sequenced motifs across trials.
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis showing above-chance mouse identification from motif sequences.

claim: A classifier trained to decode mouse identity from motif sequences performed above chance for eight out of nine mice.
source: A classifier trained to decode mouse identity from the motif sequences on a trial-by-trial basis was able to perform above chance for eight out of nine mice (Figure 6D; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Movement sequences are not statistically distinguishable across different concentration ratios.
source: Across the different concentration ratios (Figure 2D), movement sequences were not statistically distinguishable (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis showing inability to distinguish concentration ratios from motif sequences.

claim: Odor omission trials (0:0) give distinguishable motif patterns compared to other conditions.
source: The only condition that gave distinguishable motif patterns were the odor omission trials (0:0), in which the mice made longer, more tortuous trajectories (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis and trajectory analysis comparing 0:0 to other conditions.

claim: Mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner in the movement parameters measured.
source: Thus, although this model is sensitive enough to decode mouse identity (Figure 6D), it does not detect stimulus-dependent modifications of sampling behavior, suggesting that the mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner, at least in the movement parameters we measured.
evidence: Inferred from inability to decode concentration ratio from motif sequences despite ability to decode mouse identity.

claim: The absence of an adaptive strategy in response to task difficulty may be due to impulsivity.
source: We speculate that this absence of an adaptive strategy is due to impulsivity (Miyazaki et al., 2012; Fonseca et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of gradient-dependent sampling modifications, supported by citations.

claim: Clustering of motifs by transition probabilities separates them into two groups corresponding to investigation and approach states.
source: To reveal higher-order structure in the temporal organization of these motifs, we applied a clustering algorithm that minimizes the Euclidean distance between rows of the Markov transition matrix (i.e., purely based on the conditional probabilities of motifs following them). This clustering separated motifs into two groups (Figure 7A), with several distinct properties.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of transition matrix shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Investigation motifs tend to occur early in the trial, while approach motifs tend to begin later.
source: First, investigation and approach motifs cluster their onset times in the trial, with investigation motifs tending to occur early in the trial, while approach motifs tend to begin later (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of motif onset times shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Trials begin with investigation and end with approach.
source: Grouping motifs into these higher-order states shows a consistent trial sequence, with trials beginning with investigation and ending with approach (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of state sequences shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: Switches from approach back to investigation are common during trials.
source: Importantly, entering the approach state is not a final, ballistic commitment to a given water port – switches from approach back to investigation were common (Figure 7C, D, Video 7).
evidence: Supported by analysis of state transitions shown in Figure 7C, D and Video 7.

claim: Mice continuously integrate evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
source: This pattern suggests that the mice are continuously integrating evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
evidence: Inferred from observation of frequent switches between approach and investigation states.

claim: During investigation motifs, mice move more slowly and sniff more rapidly, whereas approach states are associated with faster movement and slower sniffing.
source: Second, these states correlated with distinct sniff rates and movement speeds. During investigation motifs, the mice moved more slowly and sniffed more rapidly, whereas the approach states were associated with faster movement and slower sniffing (Figure 7E) (Video 8).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sniff rate and movement speed for investigation versus approach motifs, shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms are distinct in investigation versus approach states.
source: Third, the sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms (Figures 4 and 5) were distinct in the two states (Figure 7F; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of kinematic rhythms between states, shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Nose speed and yaw velocity are more synchronized with sniffing during the investigation state than approach state.
source: Specifically, nose speed and yaw velocity are more synchronized with sniffing during the investigation state (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of kinematic modulation shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Nose speed and yaw velocity modulation differences between investigation and approach exceed what would be expected from across-trial tendencies.
source: This analysis showed that nose speed and yaw velocity modulation exceeded what would be expected from across-trial tendencies (1000 shuffles, p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by permutation testing comparing real data to shuffled controls.

claim: Z-velocity modulation differences between investigation and approach do not exceed what would be expected from across-trial tendencies.
source: while the Z-velocity modulation did not (p=0.31).
evidence: Supported by permutation testing comparing real data to shuffled controls.

claim: Switches between investigation and approach states mark behavioral inflection points that can be identified from trial to trial.
source: Switches between the investigation and approach state mark behavioral inflection points that can be identified from trial to trial.
evidence: Inferred from consistent temporal structure of state transitions across trials.

claim: Behavioral inflection points are a signature of key moments in the mouse's evolving decision process.
source: We reason that these behavioral inflection points are a signature of key moments in the mouse's evolving decision process.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal structure and properties of state transitions.

claim: The motif analysis provides a framework for temporal alignment of diverse movement trajectories with simultaneously recorded physiological data.
source: Thus, our analysis can provide a framework for temporal alignment of diverse movement trajectories with simultaneously recorded physiological data (Markowitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Proposed utility of the analysis method, supported by citation to similar approach.

claim: Investigation motif onsets occur in a precise timing relationship with sniffing.
source: For example, the onset times of motif 6 (dark blue) occurred in a precise timing relationship with sniffing (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of motif onset times relative to sniffing, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Sharp peaks in inhalation time histograms are apparent for investigation motifs, and less so for approach motifs.
source: Sharp peaks are apparent in both histograms for investigation motifs, and less so for approach motifs (quantified below; Figure 8B, C).
evidence: Supported by peristimulus time histograms shown in Figure 8B, C.

claim: Timing relationships between motif onsets and sniffing are consistent across mice.
source: Importantly, these timing relationships are consistent across mice, with some motifs tending to occur early in the sniff cycle during inhalation and others occurring later in the sniff cycle (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by cross-mouse analysis of motif onset timing shown in Figure 8D.

claim: All investigation motifs are significantly modulated in both time and phase coordinates relative to sniffing.
source: All investigation motifs were significantly modulated for both time and phase coordinates (Figure 8E; filled symbols, permutation test, p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by modulation index analysis with permutation testing, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: One approach motif is significantly modulated in time coordinates.
source: One approach motif was significantly modulated in time coordinates (Figure 8E; right-half filled symbol, p=0.003)
evidence: Supported by modulation index analysis with permutation testing, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Two approach motifs are significantly modulated in phase coordinates.
source: while two approach motifs were significantly modulated in phase coordinates (Figure 8E; left-half filled symbols, p=0.015 and p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by modulation index analysis with permutation testing, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The data are inconclusive as to whether motif onsets organize relative to sniff cycle in time versus phase.
source: Comparing the modulation indices between time and phase coordinates does not reveal a consistent pattern of modulation in time vs. phase – some motifs had higher MI in phase, others in time. Thus, our data are inconclusive as to how motif onsets organize relative to the sniff cycle.
evidence: Based on mixed results from modulation index comparisons.

claim: Kinematic inflection points synchronize with breathing during olfactory search.
source: Nevertheless, these analyses demonstrate that kinematic inflection points synchronize with breathing during olfactory search.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing significant modulation of motif onsets relative to sniffing.

claim: Breathing synchronizes to other motor and brain rhythms.
source: Given that breathing synchronizes to other motor and brain rhythms
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: Motifs correlate to the structure of activity of many neurons.
source: Given that breathing synchronizes to other motor and brain rhythms, these motifs likewise correlate to the structure of activity of many neurons.
evidence: Inferred from synchronization of motifs with breathing and known synchronization of breathing with neural activity.

claim: The motif analysis will be a useful tool to pinpoint behaviorally relevant activity in widespread brain regions.
source: Thus, our analysis will be a useful tool to pinpoint behaviorally relevant activity in widespread brain regions.
evidence: Proposed utility based on correlation of motifs with neural rhythms.

claim: Motif transition times indicate 'decision points' at which the animal chooses its next move.
source: We propose that motif transition times indicate 'decision points' at which the animal chooses its next move (Markowitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Proposed interpretation of motif transitions, supported by citation.

claim: Investigation motifs may correspond to an evidence-gathering state, while approach motifs may correspond to a reward-gathering state.
source: The transitions between investigation and approach motifs are particularly relevant since investigation motifs may correspond to an evidence-gathering state, while approach motifs may correspond to a reward-gathering state.
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on properties of investigation and approach states.

claim: Mice primarily investigate near the initiation port and primarily approach close to the decision line.
source: As expected from the temporal structure of investigation and approach (Figure 7C, D), the mice primarily investigate near the initiation port (Figure 9A; n = 9 mice) and primarily approach close to the decision line (Figure 9A, orange).
evidence: Supported by occupancy mapping analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Investigation and approach occupancy maps overlap in a region between initiation port and decision line where overall occupancy peaks.
source: Along the longitudinal axis of the arena, the two occupancy maps overlap in a region between initiation port and decision line (Figure 9A, black) where overall occupancy also peaks (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by occupancy mapping analysis shown in Figure 9A and Figure 3F.

claim: The overlap region between investigation and approach is roughly centered on the lateral midline on average across mice.
source: Along the lateral axis of the arena, on average the overlap region is roughly centered on the lateral midline between left and right sides (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by occupancy mapping analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Individual mice have their overlap region in different positions relative to the lateral midline.
source: However, this centered position is not representative of the individual mice, which have their overlap region in different positions relative to the lateral midline, with some on the left, and others on the right (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by individual mouse occupancy maps shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When trials are oriented such that the chosen side is always up, the overlap region is displaced toward the chosen side in all individual mice.
source: However, if trials are oriented such that the chosen side is always up in the occupancy maps, the overlap region is displaced toward the chosen side of the arena in all individual mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by choice-oriented occupancy maps shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice primarily switch between investigation and approach states while located on the side they would ultimately choose.
source: Thus, the mice primarily switched states while located on the side they would ultimately choose.
evidence: Inferred from displacement of overlap region toward chosen side in choice-oriented maps.

claim: Most of the change in investigation-approach index along the longitudinal axis occurs between 5 and 10 cm from the initiation port.
source: Along the longitudinal axis, most of the change in this index occurred between inflection points at 5 and 10 cm, which we define as a 'transition zone' for the analyses below (Figure 9D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of investigation-approach index shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Investigation-approach index is variably distributed across mice along the lateral axis.
source: Along the lateral axis of the arena, I.A.I. was quite variably distributed across mice, both for the entire occupancy map and within the transition zone (Figure 9E)
evidence: Supported by analysis of investigation-approach index shown in Figure 9E.

claim: When trials are oriented with respect to the chosen side, occupancy shows primarily investigation on the unchosen side and primarily approach on the chosen side.
source: Orienting trials with respect to the chosen side demonstrates a clearer pattern, with primarily investigation on the unchosen side and primarily approach on the chosen side (Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by choice-oriented occupancy analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: For a single-sniff absolute concentration strategy, the most informative location to sample is directly downwind of the odor ports.
source: For the single-sniff hypothesis, the most informative location to sample is directly downwind of the odor ports, where concentration differences between left and right trials are maximal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of odor concentration discriminability shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: For gradient sensing, the optimal location to sample is across the lateral midline, where the gradients are sharpest.
source: For gradient sensing, the optimal location is instead across the lateral midline, where the gradients are sharpest (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Yovel et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on analysis of gradient discriminability shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, supported by citation.

claim: Correct and incorrect trials yield qualitatively similar occupancy maps.
source: Correct and incorrect trials yielded qualitatively similar occupancy maps (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by visual comparison of occupancy maps shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Correct trials feature significantly higher investigation-approach index in the latter part of the transition zone.
source: Correct trials featured significantly higher I.A.I. (greater investigation) in the latter part of the transition zone, while past the decision zone the I.A.I. was higher for incorrect trials (Figure 10C; permutation test, p<0.001, n = 9 mice).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of investigation-approach index between correct and incorrect trials, shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Increased investigation in the transition zone is associated with correct trials, while increased investigation near the decision line is associated with incorrect trials.
source: Thus, increased investigation in the transition zone was associated with correct trials, while increased investigation near the decision line was associated with incorrect trials.
evidence: Supported by analysis of investigation-approach index differences between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Investigation is not inherently advantageous to olfactory search irrespective of location.
source: This pattern suggests that investigation is not inherently advantageous to olfactory search irrespective of location. Instead, it matters where the mouse investigates, and some locations are less advantageous.
evidence: Inferred from location-dependent differences in investigation between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Absolute concentrations are most discriminable near the decision line.
source: Notably, absolute concentrations are most discriminable near the decision line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by discriminability analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mice may not be able to capitalize on absolute concentration cues near the decision line under these conditions.
source: suggesting that mice may not be able to capitalize on this cue under these conditions.
evidence: Inferred from increased investigation near decision line being associated with incorrect trials despite high concentration discriminability there.

claim: Correct trials feature significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline relative to incorrect trials.
source: Correct trials featured significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline relative to incorrect trials (Figure 10G; permutation test, p<0.001, n = 9 mice).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of lateral occupancy between correct and incorrect trials, shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Occupancy of the unchosen side precedes a crossing of the midline to get to the chosen side.
source: By definition, occupancy of the unchosen side precedes a crossing of the midline to get to the chosen side.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of unchosen side in choice-oriented coordinates.

claim: There is an advantage to sampling both sides of the midline, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
source: This suggests an advantage to sampling both sides of the midline, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
evidence: Inferred from increased investigation on unchosen side being associated with correct trials.

claim: Investigation downwind of the odor port is increased on incorrect trials.
source: Further, investigation more laterally, downwind of the odor port, was increased on incorrect trials
evidence: Supported by lateral occupancy analysis comparing correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Sampling downwind of the odor port is not advantageous for task performance, contrary to the single-sniff absolute concentration hypothesis.
source: suggesting that sampling this location was not advantageous for task performance, contrary to the single-sniff absolute concentration hypothesis.
evidence: Inferred from increased investigation downwind being associated with incorrect trials.

claim: Incorrect trials show significantly higher approach occupancy at and around the midline.
source: Approach occupancy showed a different pattern, with significantly higher approach at and around the midline on incorrect trials
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of approach occupancy between correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Correct trials show a significant increase in approach occupancy closer to the chosen water port.
source: and a significant increase in approach occupancy closer to the chosen water port (Figure 10H; permutation test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of approach occupancy shown in Figure 10H.

claim: On correct trials, investigation-approach index shows significant elevation at the midline and into the unchosen side of the arena.
source: Consistent with these observations, on correct trials I.A.I. showed significant elevation at the midline and into the unchosen side of the arena
evidence: Supported by investigation-approach index analysis comparing correct and incorrect trials.

claim: Increased investigation-approach index on the chosen side is associated with incorrect trials.
source: while increased I.A.I. of the chosen side was associated with incorrect trials (Figure 10I; permutation test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by investigation-approach index analysis shown in Figure 10I.

claim: It is advantageous to sample both sides of the midline in this task, consistent with the serial-sniff hypothesis.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that it is advantageous to sample both sides of the midline in this task, consistent with the serial-sniff hypothesis.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of occupancy analysis evidence.

claim: Both stay and switch trials show significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline for correct trials.
source: Although not identical, both stay and switch trials showed significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline for correct trials (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by separate analysis of stay and switch trials shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apparent advantage of sampling across the midline is not an artifact of the asymmetry between switch and stay trials.
source: This analysis demonstrates that the apparent advantage of sampling across the midline is not an artifact of the asymmetry between switch and stay trials.
evidence: Supported by consistent results across stay and switch trial analysis.

claim: Mice use a serial-sniff strategy to sense gradient cues in this task.
source: Taken together, investigation and approach occupancy mapping provides further evidence, suggesting that mice use a serial-sniff strategy to sense gradient cues in this task (Catania, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of occupancy analysis evidence, supported by citation.

claim: Mice learn the olfactory search task in days and can perform approximately 150 trials daily for months.
source: Mice learn our behavioral task in days, after which they perform approximately 150 trials daily, sometimes for months.
evidence: Supported by training and experimental session data.

claim: Task performance worsens for shallower odor gradients at a fixed absolute concentration.
source: Task performance worsens for shallower odor gradients at a fixed absolute concentration
evidence: Supported by performance data across concentration ratio conditions (Figure 2D).

claim: Task performance is unaffected by varying absolute concentrations at a fixed concentration gradient.
source: but is unaffected by varying absolute concentrations at a fixed concentration gradient.
evidence: Supported by equal performance in 90:30 and 30:10 conditions (Figure 2E).

claim: Mice can navigate noisy gradients formed by turbulent odor plumes.
source: Taken together, these results show that mice can navigate noisy gradients formed by turbulent odor plumes.
evidence: Inferred from performance data showing gradient-guided navigation in turbulent conditions.

claim: Gradient-guided search is robust to perturbations including novel odorant introduction and naris occlusion.
source: This gradient-guided search is robust to perturbations including novel odorant introduction and naris occlusion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing maintained performance with vanillin and naris occlusion.

claim: Movement trajectories are not stereotyped, but vary considerably across trials.
source: Movement trajectories are not stereotyped, but vary considerably across trials.
evidence: Supported by trajectory analysis showing trial-to-trial variability (Figure 3D, E).

claim: The AR-HMM analysis captures common movement features across mice, but individual mice can be identified by how they sequence motifs.
source: This analysis captures common movement features across mice, but individual mice can be identified by how they sequence these motifs.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis and decoding results (Figure 6).

claim: The AR-HMM model was not constrained to find structure at a specific timescale, and consequently identified very brief, simple motifs.
source: Our model was not constrained to find structure at a specific timescale, and consequently identified very brief, simple motifs.
evidence: Based on the design and results of the AR-HMM modeling approach.

claim: Approach motifs are not ballistic commitments to an answer – switches from approach to investigation occur on many trials.
source: Even so, approach motifs are not ballistic commitments to an answer – switches from approach to investigation occurred on many trials.
evidence: Supported by analysis of state transitions (Figure 7C, D).

claim: The onset times of motifs are precisely locked to sniffing, with investigation motifs starting at characteristic phases of the sniff cycle.
source: Lastly, the onset times of motifs were precisely locked to sniffing, with investigation motifs starting at characteristic phases of the sniff cycle.
evidence: Supported by analysis of motif onset timing relative to sniffing (Figure 8).

claim: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach suggests that the investigation state is not inherently advantageous.
source: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach suggests that the investigation state is not inherently advantageous.
evidence: Inferred from location-dependent performance differences in investigation occupancy.

claim: Where the mouse investigates matters for performance.
source: Rather, where the mouse investigates matters for performance.
evidence: Inferred from spatial analysis of investigation occupancy and performance.

claim: The dependence of performance on investigation location indicates the spatial distribution of informative features in this olfactory scene.
source: This dependence of performance on location indicates the spatial distribution of informative features in this olfactory scene.
evidence: Inferred from relationship between investigation location and performance.

claim: Mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information to guide performance in this task.
source: Thus, these analyses provide further evidence that the mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information to guide performance in this task.
evidence: Inferred from increased investigation downwind (where absolute concentration is most discriminable) being associated with incorrect trials.

claim: Mice perform best when they investigate the location of the steepest slope of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
source: but rather perform best when they investigate the location of the steepest slope of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
evidence: Inferred from increased investigation at midline (where gradient is steepest) being associated with correct trials.

claim: Sampling off axis can be an optimal strategy for localization across diverse sensory systems and species.
source: Thus, our unsupervised computational analysis of airborne odor tracking supports the idea that sampling off axis can be an optimal strategy for localization across diverse sensory systems and species (Yovel et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from occupancy analysis results, supported by citation to similar finding in bats.

claim: Olfactory navigation can be either guided or gated by odor.
source: Olfactory navigation can be either guided or gated by odor (Baker et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature, supported by citation.

claim: Some organisms operate in a regime where diffusion forms smooth chemical gradients, in which classical chemotaxis strategies can be effective.
source: Some organisms operate in a regime where diffusion forms smooth chemical gradients, in which classical chemotaxis strategies can be effective (Bargmann, 2006; Berg, 2000; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Lockery, 2011).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature, supported by citations.

claim: Flying insects often operate in a highly turbulent regime where concentration gradients are not reliably informative.
source: In contrast, other organisms, such as flying insects, often operate in a highly turbulent regime where concentration gradients are not reliably informative (Crimaldi et al., 2002; Murlis et al., 1992; Riffell et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature, supported by citations.

claim: Mice in this task operate in an intermediate regime, where turbulent odor plumes close to the ground form noisy gradients.
source: By design, mice in our task operate in an intermediate regime, where turbulent odor plumes close to the ground form noisy gradients (Gire et al., 2016; Riffell et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on task design and odor measurements, supported by citations.

claim: Mice are guided by gradient cues in the intermediate turbulent regime.
source: Because behavior varies with the gradient and not the absolute concentration (Figure 2C–E), we have shown that mice are guided by gradient cues in this regime.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing gradient-dependent but not absolute concentration-dependent performance.

claim: Performance is higher when mice sample both sides of the midline, suggesting they sense the gradient by comparing sniff sequences across time.
source: Further, performance is higher when the mice sample both sides of the midline, suggesting that they sense the gradient by comparing sniff sequences across time.
evidence: Inferred from occupancy analysis showing advantage of sampling across midline.

claim: Previous studies of olfactory navigation in depositional odor trails showed that stereo manipulations had small but significant effects on performance and led to changes in movement strategy.
source: This finding contrasts with previous studies of olfactory navigation in a different regime: following a depositional odor trail. In these studies, stereo manipulations had small but significant effects on performance, and led to changes in movement strategy (Jones and Urban, 2018; Khan et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: In moles, stereo reversal did not affect navigation at a distance from the target, but reversed turning behavior in the target's immediate vicinity.
source: Importantly, a study of olfactory search in moles showed that stereo reversal did not affect navigation at a distance from the target, but reversed turning behavior in the target's immediate vicinity (Catania, 2013).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Stereo cues may be informative near a source where gradients are steep, but play less of a role at greater distance from the source where gradients are more shallow.
source: These results suggest that stereo cues may be informative near a source, where gradients are steep, but that stereo cues play less of a role at a greater distance from the source where gradients are more shallow.
evidence: Inferred from previous literature on stereo olfaction in different spatial regimes.

claim: Serial-sniff comparisons have been hypothesized as a potential sensory computation for odor gradient following at a distance from the source.
source: In this more distant condition, serial-sniff comparisons have been hypothesized as a potential sensory computation for odor gradient following Catania, 2013.
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: The task design forces mice out of the stereo regime and into the serial-sniff comparison regime.
source: We propose that our task design, in which mice must commit to a side at a distance from the source, forces mice out of the stereo regime and into the serial-sniff comparison regime.
evidence: Proposed explanation for lack of stereo effects, based on task design and results.

claim: Neurons sensitive to sniff-to-sniff odor concentration changes have been observed in the olfactory bulb of head-fixed mice.
source: Neurons sensitive to sniff-to-sniff odor concentration changes have been observed in the olfactory bulb of head-fixed mice (Parabucki et al., 2019), providing a potential physiological mechanism for this sensory computation.
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Physiological mechanisms revealed in head-fixed mice may not generalize to the freely moving search condition.
source: On the other hand, physiological mechanisms revealed in head-fixed mice may not generalize to the freely moving search condition.
evidence: Cautionary statement about generalization from head-fixed to freely moving conditions.

claim: The external stimulus obtained by moving the nose through a noisy gradient differs dramatically from the square odor pulses delivered during head-fixed or odor-poke olfactory tasks.
source: The external stimulus obtained by moving the nose through a noisy gradient differs dramatically from the square odor pulses delivered during head-fixed or odor-poke olfactory tasks.
evidence: Comparison of stimulus conditions between freely moving and head-fixed paradigms.

claim: The sniff statistics observed in freely moving mice are qualitatively faster than those reported in head-fixed mice under most conditions.
source: Further, the sniff statistics we observe in our mice are qualitatively faster than those reported in head-fixed mice under most conditions (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison of sniff rates between freely moving and head-fixed conditions, supported by citations.

claim: Mice sniff fast in response to a novel odor.
source: One exception is that mice sniff fast in response to a novel odor (Wesson et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Fast stimulation impacts the responsiveness of olfactory sensory neurons.
source: Such fast stimulation impacts the responsiveness of olfactory sensory neurons (Esclassan et al., 2012; Ghatpande and Reisert, 2011; Verhagen et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Short- and long-term synaptic and network plasticity mechanisms influence the olfactory bulb's responses during fast sniffing.
source: In addition to the temporal properties of odor transduction, short- and long-term synaptic and network plasticity mechanisms will influence the olfactory bulb's responses during fast sniffing (Beshel et al., 2007; Díaz-Quesada et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2015; Jordan et al., 2018; Mandairon and Linster, 2009; Patterson et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement of knowledge from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Without tapping into the fast sniffing regime, the understanding gained from head-fixed studies in olfaction will be incomplete at best.
source: Without tapping into the fast sniffing regime, the understanding we can gain from head-fixed studies in olfaction will be incomplete at best.
evidence: Argument for importance of studying freely moving behavior, based on differences from head-fixed conditions.

claim: It is necessary to complement well-controlled reductionist behavioral paradigms with less-controlled, more natural paradigms.
source: In the future, it will be necessary to complement well-controlled reductionist behavioral paradigms with less-controlled, more natural paradigms like ours.
evidence: Proposed methodological approach for future research.

claim: Mice execute a strategic behavioral program when searching, synchronizing fast sniffing with three-dimensional head movements at a tens of milliseconds timescale.
source: Mice execute a strategic behavioral program when searching, synchronizing fast sniffing with three-dimensional head movements at a tens of milliseconds timescale.
evidence: Summary of main finding supported by experimental data (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: Rodents investigate their environment with active sniffing and whisking behaviors.
source: It has long been known that rodents investigate their environment with active sniffing and whisking behaviors (Kepecs et al., 2006; Wachowiak, 2011; Welker, 1964).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature, supported by citations.

claim: Under some conditions, sniffing locks with whisking, nose twitches, and head movement on a cycle-by-cycle basis.
source: More recent work has established that under some conditions sniffing locks with whisking, nose twitches, and head movement on a cycle-by-cycle basis (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2013; Ranade et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Sniffing synchronizes with brain oscillations in olfactory regions, hippocampus, amygdala, and neocortex.
source: Sniffing also synchronizes with brain oscillations not only in olfactory regions, but also in hippocampus, amygdala, and neocortex (Karalis and Sirota, 2018; Kay, 2005; Macrides et al., 1982; Vanderwolf, 1992; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Zelano et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Respiratory central pattern generators may coordinate sampling movements to synchronize sensory dynamics across modalities with internal brain rhythms.
source: Respiratory central pattern generators may coordinate sampling movements to synchronize sensory dynamics across modalities with internal brain rhythms (Kleinfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: Proposed mechanism from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Locomotor and facial movement, which are often synchronized to respiration, drive activity in numerous brain regions, including primary sensory areas.
source: Further, locomotor and facial movement, which are often synchronized to respiration, drive activity in numerous brain regions, including primary sensory areas (McGinley et al., 2015; Musall et al., 2019; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: In the real world, sensory receptors operate in closed loop with movement.
source: In the real world, sensory receptors operate in closed loop with movement (Ahissar and Assa, 2016; Gibson, 1966).
evidence: Statement of established principle from literature, supported by citations.

claim: Sensory systems must disambiguate self-induced stimulus dynamics from changes in the environment.
source: Consequently, sensory systems must disambiguate self-induced stimulus dynamics from changes in the environment.
evidence: Logical inference from closed-loop nature of sensory-motor interaction.

claim: Active sampling movements can provide access to sensory information that is not otherwise available to a stationary observer.
source: Further, active sampling movements can provide access to sensory information that is not otherwise available to a stationary observer (Gibson, 1962; Schroeder et al., 2010; Yarbus, 1967).
evidence: Statement of principle from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Widespread movement-related signals may allow the brain to compensate for and capitalize on self-induced stimulus dynamics.
source: Widespread movement-related signals may allow the brain to compensate for and capitalize on self-induced stimulus dynamics (Poulet and Hedwig, 2006; Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Sperry, 1950; von Holst and Mittelstaedt, 1950; Webb, 2004).
evidence: Proposed function of movement-related signals, supported by citations.

claim: Recent developments in machine vision, deep learning, and probabilistic generative modeling make rigorously quantifying the behavior of freely moving animals more feasible than ever.
source: Rigorously quantifying the behavior of freely moving animals is more feasible than ever, thanks to recent developments in machine vision, deep learning, and probabilistic generative modeling (Datta et al., 2019; Gomez-Marin et al., 2014; Mathis and Mathis, 2020), as our work shows.
evidence: Statement about methodological advances, supported by citations and demonstrated by current work.

claim: The motifs defined by AR-HMM provide a compact description of the behavior, while still capturing the idiosyncrasies of individual mice.
source: In particular, the motifs we have defined provide a compact description of the behavior, while still capturing the idiosyncrasies of individual mice.
evidence: Summary of motif analysis properties demonstrated in results.

claim: Two-state search strategies are common across phylogeny.
source: Two-state search strategies are common across phylogeny (Bargmann, 2006; Berg, 2000; Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; Lockery, 2011; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014; Vickers and Baker, 1994).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature, supported by citations.

claim: In smaller organisms, state switches have provided a useful behavioral readout for understanding the neural mechanisms of odor-guided behavior.
source: In smaller organisms, state switches have provided a useful behavioral readout for understanding the neural mechanisms of odor-guided behavior (Bi and Sourjik, 2018; Larsch et al., 2015; Baker et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of findings from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: Where switches between investigation and approach occur in allocentric space can reveal the location of informative features in an olfactory scene.
source: Here, we have shown that where switches between investigation and approach occur in allocentric space can reveal the location of informative features in an olfactory scene.
evidence: Summary of finding from occupancy analysis.

claim: The transition points between 'investigation' and 'approach' serve as a principled template against which to compare neural activity.
source: The transition points between 'investigation' and 'approach' serve as a principled template against which to compare neural activity.
evidence: Proposed utility of the analysis for future neural studies.

claim: This work establishes a framework for studying neural mechanisms of active sensing in an unrestrained mammal.
source: Our work thus establishes a framework for studying neural mechanisms of active sensing in an unrestrained mammal.
evidence: Summary of contribution of the work.
